concepts.name: Article 323-A: Administrative Tribunals — Constitutional Basis and Scope
key_dimensions: Inserted by 42nd Amendment 1976 — origin, intent, and the Swaran Singh Committee recommendation
Scope: covers recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services — what is included vs. excluded (e.g., armed forces, Supreme Court/HC staff)
Parliament's exclusive power to establish CAT vs. States' role — distinction from Article 323-B
Whether jurisdiction of High Courts is fully ousted — L. Chandra Kumar case reversal of S.P. Sampath Kumar ruling

concepts.name: Article 323-B: Tribunals for Other Matters — Scope and Legislative Competence
key_dimensions: 14 specific subjects listed (taxation, foreign exchange, industrial/labour disputes, land reforms, ceiling on urban property, elections, food, rent) — which Parliament AND State Legislatures can legislate upon
Key distinction from 323-A: both Parliament and State Legislatures can create tribunals under 323-B; only Parliament under 323-A
Clause allowing exclusion of jurisdiction of all courts except Supreme Court — constitutional tension with basic structure
Overlap trap: which tribunal is created under which Article — e.g., NGT is NOT under 323-B but under a statutory Act

concepts.name: Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) — Structure, Jurisdiction, and Limitations
key_dimensions: Established under Administrative Tribunals Act 1985 pursuant to Article 323-A — original jurisdiction over service matters of Central Government employees
Composition: Chairman (retired SC/HC judge) + Administrative and Judicial Members — qualifications and appointment controversy
Exclusions from CAT's jurisdiction: Supreme Court staff, armed forces personnel, officers of Parliament secretariats — UPSC trap on who is NOT covered
Appeals from CAT go to Division Bench of High Court (post L. Chandra Kumar), not directly to Supreme Court — procedural sequence

concepts.name: L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997) — Judicial Review of Tribunal Orders
key_dimensions: 7-judge Constitution Bench ruling: clauses excluding High Court jurisdiction under Articles 323-A and 323-B are unconstitutional as they violate basic structure (judicial review)
Overruled S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) which had upheld total ouster of HC jurisdiction as valid substitution
Established that tribunal orders are subject to judicial review by Division Bench of concerned High Court under Articles 226/227
Implication: tribunals are supplemental, not substitutes, for High Courts — doctrinal significance for all tribunal types

concepts.name: Rojer Mathew Case (2019) — Tribunal Reforms and Appointment Rules
key_dimensions: 5-judge bench referred question of tribunals' constitutional validity to larger bench; interim directions on Tribunal, Appellate Tribunal and Other Authorities (Qualification, Experience and Other Conditions of Service of Members) Rules 2017
Core issue: executive dominance in tribunal appointments compromising independence — separation of powers dimension
Court struck down provisions allowing short tenures, re-appointment, and government control over service conditions
Led to Tribunals Reforms (Rationalisation and Conditions of Service) Act 2021 — abolition of several tribunals and merger with courts

concepts.name: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 — Rationalization and Abolition of Tribunals
key_dimensions: Abolished 9 tribunals/appellate bodies including IPAB, Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, Airport Appellate Tribunal — transferred jurisdiction to High Courts
Fixed 4-year term for Chairperson and Members (minimum age 50) — Supreme Court's objection to short terms
Search-cum-Selection Committee composition controversy: government nominees forming majority — independence concern
Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2021): Supreme Court struck down provisions on 4-year term and 50-year age limit as unconstitutional — ongoing tension

concepts.name: National Green Tribunal (NGT) — Statutory Basis, Jurisdiction, and Unique Features
key_dimensions: Established under NGT Act 2010 — NOT under Article 323-B; derives power from Parliament's competence under Articles 253 and Entry 13 List I (international obligations — Stockholm, Rio principles)
Jurisdiction: substantial question relating to environment including enforcement of legal right — 'substantial question' threshold trap
Original jurisdiction + appellate jurisdiction over orders of regulatory bodies — dual nature
NGT has power to award compensation and restitution — quasi-civil court powers; appeals lie to Supreme Court directly (not HC) — major procedural distinction

concepts.name: Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) — Constitutional Position and Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Established under Armed Forces Tribunal Act 2007 — adjudicates service matters and appeals from court martial decisions
Exclusion from Article 323-A scope: armed forces personnel are explicitly excluded — hence AFT created under ordinary legislative power (Article 246 + Union List Entry 2)
Appeals from AFT go directly to Supreme Court under Article 136 — High Courts have NO jurisdiction (unlike CAT); this is a critical UPSC trap
Composition: retired SC judge as Chairman + retired High Court judges and military members — civil-military balance in composition

concepts.name: Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) — Oldest Tribunal and Its Significance
key_dimensions: Established in 1941 under Income Tax Act — oldest quasi-judicial tribunal in India, predating constitutional provisions on tribunals
Final fact-finding authority — questions of fact do not go further; only substantial questions of law go to High Court under Section 260A
Not established under Article 323-B — created under ordinary statute; Article 323-B provides constitutional sanction for such tribunals retrospectively
Composition: Judicial Members (HC judges or advocates) + Accountant Members (CA/IRS officers) — techno-legal hybrid model

concepts.name: Distinction Between Tribunal and Court — Constitutional and Functional Criteria
key_dimensions: Key tests from Bharat Bank v. Employees (1950) and Associated Cement v. P.N. Sharma (1965): state power, binding decisions, procedural trappings of court
Tribunal need not follow CPC/Evidence Act strictly — flexible procedure; but must follow principles of natural justice
Tribunal can have non-judicial technical members (expert members); courts must be presided over by legally trained persons
Constitutional status: tribunals are NOT courts subordinate to High Courts under Article 227 in the strict sense — but post-L. Chandra Kumar, HC can supervise via Articles 226/227

concepts.name: Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) — Jurisdiction Over SEBI, IRDAI, and PFRDA Orders
key_dimensions: Established under SEBI Act 1992 — appellate jurisdiction over orders of SEBI; later extended to IRDAI and PFRDA orders
Presided by retired SC judge or Chief Justice of HC — higher judicial calibre requirement than many other tribunals
Appeals from SAT go to Supreme Court directly on questions of law — bypasses High Court, similar to AFT (UPSC trap: not all tribunal appeals go to HC)
Distinction: SAT hears appeals against regulatory orders, not service matters — subject-matter jurisdiction contrast with CAT

concepts.name: National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and NCLAT — Consolidation of Corporate Adjudication
key_dimensions: NCLT established under Companies Act 2013 — replaced Company Law Board, BIFR, AAIFR, and part of HC jurisdiction (winding up)
Constitutional validity challenged: Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010) SC upheld NCLT but struck down several provisions on judicial member qualifications and executive control
NCLAT is appellate body over NCLT + CCI orders (competition matters) — dual appellate role is a distinguishing feature
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 vests adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency in NCLT — new critical jurisdiction post-2016

concepts.name: Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) and DRAT — Banking Sector Adjudication
key_dimensions: Established under Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act 1993 — for speedy recovery of dues above ₹20 lakh (now ₹10 lakh threshold modified)
Presiding Officer must be a District Judge or equivalent — exclusively judicial composition (unlike mixed tribunals)
SARFAESI Act 2002 expanded DRT's role — borrowers can appeal against bank action to DRT within 45 days
Constitutional challenge: Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2004) — SC upheld DRT's validity as High Court alternative for specific commercial disputes

concepts.name: Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) — Regulatory Adjudication Model
key_dimensions: Established under TRAI Act 1997 (amended 2000) — adjudicates disputes between licensor/licensee, service providers, and between providers and consumers (above individual level)
TRAI (regulator) and TDSAT (adjudicator) separation — regulatory and adjudicatory functions bifurcated to ensure independence; model studied for other sectors
Appeals from TDSAT lie to Supreme Court — not High Court (another bypass-HC instance)
Chairperson: retired SC judge or retired Chief Justice of HC — qualification standard ensures judicial credibility in technical domain

concepts.name: Article 136 and Tribunals — Special Leave Petition as Safety Valve
key_dimensions: Article 136 allows Supreme Court to grant SLP against any tribunal order — acts as constitutional safety valve ensuring ultimate judicial oversight
Some tribunal statutes explicitly route appeals to SC (SAT, AFT, TDSAT) — these are statutory routes distinct from discretionary Article 136
SC's power under Article 136 cannot be curtailed by any statute or Article 323-A/323-B — affirmed in L. Chandra Kumar
Difference between statutory appeal to SC (right-based) and SLP (discretionary) — important procedural distinction for Prelims

concepts.name: Independence of Tribunals — Appointment, Tenure, and Removal Controversies
key_dimensions: Core tension: tribunals under executive ministries for administrative/financial control vs. need for judicial independence — Ministry of Finance controls most economic tribunals
Supreme Court's repeated directions: Search Committee should have majority of judiciary nominees; fixed non-renewable terms to prevent re-appointment pressure
Madras Bar Association series of cases (2010, 2014, 2021) — progressive judicial assertion on independence standards
Comparison with constitutional bodies: unlike SC/HC judges, tribunal members can be removed more easily — erosion of security of tenure argument

concepts.name: Lok Adalats and Their Distinction from Tribunals
key_dimensions: Established under Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 — NOT a tribunal in constitutional sense; award is a decree of civil court but based on consent/compromise
Permanent Lok Adalats (PLAs) under 2002 amendment for public utility services — can give binding award even without consent (quasi-tribunal character), unlike regular Lok Adalats
No appeal lies against Lok Adalat award — distinguishes it from tribunal orders which are appellable; only writ jurisdiction available
UPSC trap: Lok Adalat award is deemed decree of civil court executable as such — but no court fee refund provision for PLA unlike regular Lok Adalat

concepts.name: Quasi-Judicial Bodies vs. Tribunals — Definitional Boundaries
key_dimensions: Quasi-judicial bodies (SEBI, CCI, RBI enforcement) exercise adjudicatory functions but are primarily regulatory — their orders are typically appealed to a tribunal
Tribunals are created specifically for adjudication; quasi-judicial bodies have adjudication as incidental to regulation — functional distinction
Principles of natural justice apply to both — audi alteram partem and nemo judex in causa sua — but procedural rigor differs
UPSC trap: CCI is a quasi-judicial body whose orders go to NCLAT (tribunal) — multi-tier structure; distinguishing the tier at which entity sits

concepts.name: State Administrative Tribunals (SATs) — Article 323-A(1)(b) and Federal Dimension
key_dimensions: Article 323-A empowers Parliament to establish SATs for State government employees — but requires State's consent/request (not unilateral)
Only a few States have SATs (Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Maharashtra) — not all States; awareness of which States have them
Joint Administrative Tribunals (JATs) can be established for two or more States — cooperative federalism dimension
Appeals from SAT: post-L. Chandra Kumar, lie to Division Bench of respective High Court — unlike CAT whose appeals go to HC of respective jurisdiction

concepts.name: 42nd Constitutional Amendment and Tribunals — Historical and Structural Context
key_dimensions: 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part XIV-A (Articles 323-A and 323-B) — Emergency-era origin raises questions about democratic legitimacy and executive intent to bypass courts
Also curtailed HC jurisdiction simultaneously — part of broader pattern of judiciary-clipping during Emergency
Post-Emergency, Janata government's 43rd and 44th Amendments restored some safeguards but Part XIV-A was retained — selective reversal
Swaran Singh Committee (1976) originally recommended tribunals to reduce HC backlog — original intent vs. actual implementation trajectory
